An observable-evidence rubric, full-information ablation, and human baseline under identical information constraints are essential.

The central expression–detection mismatch compares different quantities: CTAR measures the prevalence of any trait, whereas OTDA measures exact agreement across all five labels. Their numerical difference does not establish that models are better at facilitating crime than preventing it. Model-specific evaluation corpora further confound detection rankings with statement difficulty and prevalence. An all-neutral baseline and a common corpus evaluated by every detector are missing; these are particularly important for interpreting the negative CTAR–OTDA correlation.

The construct validity of 'criminal potential' remains insufficiently established. Human psychological scales are mapped to sentence-level labels without demonstrating that these labels predict meaningful misuse capability. Generated THOUGHT text is treated as evidence of intent, although it is prompted character narration. Psychological Manipulation additionally requires causing a target to change decisions, which the sentence-level evaluation does not establish. The human audit supports agreement with the proposed annotations, but does not resolve these validity issues.

Several numerical claims conflict with the reported tables. Section 4.2 states that CTAR exceeds 50% for every model, but Table 8 places GPT-4o and Qwen2.5 below 50% in both conditions. Table 10 normalizes by total trait assignments rather than sentence counts: GPT-4o’s manipulation value is 439/886, although Table 8 reports 1,650 sentences. These values measure label composition, so their interpretation as activation rates is misleading. Table 11’s combined detection accuracy is 45.99%; approximately 44% applies only to the instruction condition.

The evidence does not support the breadth of the generalization claims. Sixty scenarios derived from ten films provide limited independent diversity, and failure to identify a source film does not eliminate memorized plot influence. No repeated-run variability or uncertainty accounting for sentences clustered within scenarios and films is reported. Likewise, testing five criminal personas does not establish that detection limitations are inherent to models or broadly insensitive to prompting.

The contribution needs stronger positioning against existing interactive deception and multi-agent mystery evaluations, beyond introducing a new taxonomy and perspective arrangement. Reproducibility is also incomplete: 'default inference settings' leaves important parameters unspecified, most model identifiers lack fixed versions, sentence segmentation and failed-output handling are unclear, and the claimed dataset/framework release has no identifiable access link in the manuscript.
